verified.singer: Elisabeth Schumann, soprano (b. 13 June 1888, Merseburg; d. 23 April 1952, New York)
verified.pianist: Gerald Moore (the YouTube/Naxos metadata credit 'George Reeves' on the Topic upload is an album-metadata error; disc label and CHARM credit Moore)
verified.recording_date: 26 November 1936, London (HMV, matrix 0EA 4491-1, take 1, 78rpm disc DA 1547, coupled with Fischerweise 0EA 4490-1). NOT 26 Nov 1945 — the CHARM/archive.org metadata carries a year typo (day/month identical, year wrong): matrices 0EA 4486-4490 from the same session are all dated 1936-11-26 in the same CHARM collection, and Schumann's real 1945 sessions used matrices 0EA 10580+ (Aug 1945). She recorded Gretchen only once; all circulating transfers run ~3:26-3:32.
verified.album_label: Original: HMV DA 1547 (10-inch 78, issued 1937), from the 26.XI.1936 Abbey Road session with Gerald Moore
verified.reissues: HMV LP 'Schubert Songs Volume 1' (1962, side track 7 keeps the Fischerweise/Gretchen coupling); Naxos Historical 8.110731 'Elisabeth Schumann: Schubert Lieder (1927-1945)' (2002, the project's cited reissue); EMI 6CD 'Elisabeth Schumann - Silver Thread of Song' (CD1 tr.21) and Japanese 'Elisabeth Schumann EMI Recordings' 6CD; free CHARM FLAC transfer at archive.org/details/78_gretchen-am-spinnrade_schumann-elisabeth-moore-gerald; various gray-market digital compilations (Codex 'Best Opera Singers VIII', Classique Perfecto 'Opera Classics', M.A.T. 'The Art of Schubert Lieder', BNF Collection from a 1963 French LP)

age_voice: She was 48 (born 13 June 1888) — not 57 as the task premise assumed; the 1945 date is a metadata typo for 1936 (see concerns). In November 1936 she was still a member of the Vienna State Opera (star there 1919-1938, left only after the Anschluss) and in the middle of her most productive HMV recording period: ClassicsToday notes 23 of the 28 songs on the Naxos disc were recorded 1932-1937, 'when Schumann was in her mid-40s'. So this is a late-prime document, clearly fresher than her genuinely late sides (Aug 1945, 1946, 1948-49, ages 57-61). That said, hers was always a light, silvery soubrette-lyric instrument, and by the mid-1930s reviewers hear some age even here: ClassicsToday finds that on these 1930s sides the 'high, silvery soprano sometimes sounds fragile and technically ill-at-ease', with scooping intruding on the line and a 'woefully weak' lower register — the register Gretchen's brooding opening lives in. Lotte Lehmann's famous tribute ('perhaps the purest singing style of German lieder') and Wikipedia's note that her freshness 'never failed her, even as she entered her sixties' describe the artistry, not raw vocal power, which was never large.
reception: Lasting reputation: Elisabeth Schumann is a canonical, universally loved pre-war Schubertian — the project's #2 priority woman — and her 1930s HMV Schubert series is a classic of the catalogue; this is not label PR but a standing verdict of 90 years of collecting. BUT the specific standing of her Gretchen is second-tier within the song's discography: (1) klassik-prisma.de's 28-version comparison gives her 4 stars (1936, EMI, timing 3'20) with no prose paragraph, below the 5-star tier of Schwarzkopf/Fischer 1952, Schwarzkopf/Parsons 1973, Ludwig/Parsons, Janowitz/Gage and Zomer/Schoonderwoerd; (2) the tablecoute.blogspot.com March 2020 blind panel of eight versions did NOT include her (winners: Schwarzkopf/Fischer and Fink/Huber); (3) ClassicsToday's review of Naxos 8.110731 says explicitly: 'She wisely chose her programs to fit her vocal limitations, though Gretchen am Spinnrade really does need a bigger voice and more dramatic impetus', while granting that 'her trump card was charm... not the sickly kind laid on with a trowel'. Gramophone has a review of the same Naxos disc ('Elisabeth Schumann sings Schubert Lieder') but it is paywalled — text not retrieved. Net: a beloved singer's charming, historically important reading of a song that critics consistently judge to be outside her vocal Fach; nobody ranks this Gretchen among the greatest Gretchens.

youtube.notes: Best provenance: 'Provided to YouTube by NAXOS of America' from exactly the cited reissue, 'Schumann, Elisabeth: Schubert Lieder (1927-1945)', P 2002 Naxos (8.110731). 3:32, 173 views. Caveat: track metadata mis-credits 'George Reeves' as artist — the pianist on this side is Gerald Moore (Moore plays tracks 15-23 of the Naxos disc; Gretchen is tr.18). Clean professional Naxos Historical transfer.
Description reads 'London, 1936' — correctly dated. 3:29, 727 views, uploaded 1 Nov 2022. Duration matches the CHARM disc transfer (210.6 s), so same recording.
Description: 'Elisabeth Schumann--Soprano / Gerald Moore--Piano / 1936'. 3:32, 240 views. Long-standing historical-vocal fan channel.
Gray-market source: 'The Art of Schubert Lieder', P 2008 M.A.T. Music Theme Licensing, via The Orchard. 3:30, 61 views. Same recording, but licensing provenance inferior to the Naxos upload.
Gray-market 'Opera Classics' (Classique Perfecto, 2012). 3:29, 52 views. Confirms Moore credit but low-grade compilation source.
BNF Collection (Believe SAS) digitization of a 1963 French LP 'Schubert: Melodies (Mono Version)'. 3:26, 4 views. Same recording, likely faster transfer/trimmed; archival curiosity.

Reference-grade free FLAC of the original 78 (DA 1547, 0EA 4491-1), 3:30; the item's '1945-11-26' date field is the year typo discussed in concerns. Useful as the project's source-of-truth audio even though it is not a YouTube embed.

concerns: 1) DATE ERROR IN PROJECT NOTES AND TASK PREMISE: the '26 Nov 1945, age 57, late career' framing is wrong. The archive.org/CHARM item's date '1945-11-26' is a year typo for 26 November 1936 — proven by matrix chronology (0EA 4486-4490 same session, all 1936-11-26; the disc's own B-side Fischerweise 0EA 4490-1 is dated 1936; real 1945 sessions used 0EA 10580+), and corroborated by klassik-prisma (1936), two independent fan uploads ('London, 1936') and ClassicsToday's session summary. planning/research/schubert-singers.md line 490 repeats the 1945 error and should be corrected before publication; verify whether the Naxos 8.110731 booklet also prints 1945 (booklet PDF not retrieved). 2) The previously 'verified' YouTube ID rvGQYOkkeSQ is dead (oEmbed returns Not Found) — remove it from project notes. 3) The best-provenance upload (-IBB3bznOnQ, Naxos) mis-credits George Reeves in its metadata; if used on the site, credit Gerald Moore per disc label/CHARM. 4) Gramophone's review of the Naxos disc is paywalled — its text was not read. 5) klassik-prisma gives only a table rating (4 stars), no prose. 6) Small residual risk of an undiscovered second Schumann Gretchen (e.g., US Victor), but no trace found in DAHR/CHARM searches and all circulating transfers match one ~3:30 performance. 7) 1936 78rpm sound: perfectly listenable HMV studio quality, but surface noise varies between the fan transfers; the Naxos/Obert-Thorn-style professional transfer or the CHARM FLAC is preferable.
verdict: CASE FOR: she is the project's #2 named priority woman; this is an old master's recording — the earliest of any priority singer's Gretchen (1936 beats Lehmann ~1941, Ferrier 1947, Schwarzkopf 1952, Ludwig 1960s, Popp 1983), satisfying both the 'old masters preferred' and 'earlier wins' rules; and contrary to the task premise it is NOT a decline-era document — at 48 she was still a Vienna State Opera artist in her late prime, and this side closes her classic 1932-37 HMV Schubert series with real charm and lovely silvery tone. Availability is good: an official Naxos-distributed Topic upload plus solid fan transfers and a free reference FLAC. CASE AGAINST: independent critics consistently judge the performance, not just the singer — klassik-prisma rates it 4/5, below five 5-star versions; ClassicsToday states flatly that Gretchen 'really does need a bigger voice and more dramatic impetus' than hers; the 2020 blind panel didn't even shortlist it; her lower register (where the song broods) was weak even in 1936. As a Gretchen it is a period charmer, not a summit — the historic-era slot could arguably serve the song better with Lehmann's more dramatic ~1941 version, though Lehmann is not a named priority. VERDICT: legitimate candidate for slot 3-5 as the pre-war/old-master representative, clearly behind Schwarzkopf/Fischer 1952 (and behind Ludwig among priority singers); include if the top-5 wants a 78rpm-era voice and the named-priority weighting is applied strictly; exclude only if artistic consensus per-song outweighs singer priority. STRENGTH: 6/10.

verified.singer: Christa Ludwig, mezzo-soprano (b. 16 March 1928, Berlin - d. 24 April 2021)
verified.recording_date: 8 November 1965, Abbey Road Studio No. 1, London (per session data in the Warner 'Complete Recitals' box, CD 4 tr. 7: '8 XI.1965'). DATE DISCREPANCY RESOLVED: the EMI recital LP was compiled from sessions 28-30 Nov 1961, 20 Feb 1962, 8 Nov 1965 and 28 Jun 1966 - klassik-prisma's '1961' is the album's earliest session year, tablecoute's '1967' is the original ℗/LP publication year; the Gretchen track itself was taped 8 Nov 1965. Residual caveat: the per-track date comes from box documentation reproduced on a blog (Discogs returned 403), so 1965-11-08?
verified.album_label: LP 'Schubert Lieder', EMI/HMV, ℗ 1967 Parlophone (Discogs shows a 1968 LP release); producer of the sessions later credited as Suvi Raj Grubb
verified.reissues: EMI 'Great Recordings of the Century': 'Schubert: 15 Lieder' (2004, remaster Ian Jones, 724356289628, Gretchen = tr. 10); 'Les Introuvables de Christa Ludwig' (EMI 4CD, 1957-69 sessions); Warner 'Christa Ludwig - The Complete Recitals' 11-CD box (2018 remaster, CD 4 tr. 7)

age_voice: Ludwig was 37 at the 8 Nov 1965 session - her absolute vocal prime. The mid-1960s were her peak decade (Vienna State Opera centrepiece, the Karajan/Bernstein years); obituaries and her own memoir record that vocal-cord damage came only in the EARLY 1970s ("capillaries bursting on my vocal cords" amid divorce and menopause, forcing cancelled seasons - NYT-sourced obituary material via classicalmusicguide.com and Wikipedia). That crisis window coincides with her DG remake of Gretchen with Irwin Gage (rec. ~1973, ℗ 1974, DG 2530 404), and klassik-prisma's criticism of that remake - she "forciert bei f-Stellen in hoher Lage sehr" (forces heavily in high forte passages), "unschöne Tremoli" - matches the biography exactly. The 1965 EMI version therefore captures the voice at its best; the 1974 DG version captures it just past the break.
reception: Independent, lasting reputation - not just PR. (1) klassik-prisma.de's 28-version comparison gives Ludwig/Parsons 5 stars, in the top tier alongside Schwarzkopf 1952 and 1973, Janowitz 1977 and Zomer 2002; her DG/Gage remake gets only 4 stars with specific vocal criticism (forced high forte, unattractive tremolo). (2) tablecoute.blogspot.com's 2020 blind panel (8 versions; the Ludwig/Parsons entered as 'EMI 1967') did NOT pick her as winner (Fink/Huber and Schwarzkopf/Fischer won), but one juror ranked her second: "au bord des larmes, son timbre me touche toujours" - i.e. she held her own blind against the field. (3) EMI canonized the recital in 'Great Recordings of the Century' (2004) - a curated label series, so partly self-promotion, but historically a respected canon marker. (4) Classics Today calls her "a radiant Schubert... lieder singer" in this EMI material (general, not Gretchen-specific). No standalone Gramophone review of the GROC issue could be retrieved (archive paywalled/403). Her darker mezzo Gretchen is repeatedly singled out as the most dramatic low-voice version in the 5-star tier - all other 5-star versions are sopranos.

youtube.notes: Provided by Warner Classics from 'The Complete Recitals on Warner Classics', ℗ 1967 / 2018 remaster - the newest transfer. Credits Geoffrey Parsons explicitly. Duration 3:14 (194 s), ~21,100 views. Recommended primary embed.

Provided by Warner Classics from 'Schubert: 15 Lieder' (GROC), ℗ 1967, 2004 - Ian Jones remaster, producer credit Suvi Raj Grubb. Duration 3:13 (193 s), ~680 views. Good backup of the same recording, older remaster.
Fan upload labeled 'Geoffrey Parsons, 1965' but runs 5:04 - likely contains extra material; contents not verified, ~77 views. Do not use while Topic uploads exist.

WARNING - NOT this recording: this is the DG/Gage remake (℗ 1974, from 'The Essentials'), 3:28. Listed only to prevent mix-ups; same warning applies to 2zYJ5Z2trfc ('Schubert: Lieder', DG 1991 reissue). Near-identical titles on the same Topic channel.

concerns: (1) The per-track session date 8 Nov 1965 rests on Warner box documentation reproduced on classicalpippo9.blogspot.com plus one corroborating search summary; Discogs and Gramophone blocked direct fetches (403), so it is high-confidence but not sealed by a primary source. (2) Published sources disagree on the headline date (klassik-prisma: 1961; tablecoute: 1967); the site should say "recorded 8 Nov 1965, released 1967" to avoid propagating either error. (3) Attribution risk on YouTube is real: the same Topic channel hosts the 1974 DG/Gage remake under an almost identical title - the videoId must be locked to PCNGae1wYxU (or DAczOwKZmyY), never picked by title. (4) Topic uploads are auto-generated: they can be region-restricted in some territories and can be remapped/taken down on catalogue changes; embeddability was not directly tested. (5) The 2020 blind panel did not rank her first - her standing is top-tier, not unanimous winner. (6) No independent Gramophone-archive review was retrievable to add a third fully independent critical source.
verdict: STRONG INCLUDE - strength 9/10. Case for: Ludwig is a named priority singer; this is an old-master recording (1965) at her exact vocal prime (age 37, six years before her documented vocal-cord crisis); klassik-prisma places it in the 5-star top tier of 28 versions - the only mezzo there; it survived a 2020 blind panel with distinction; it is available in an official 2018 Warner remaster on the auto-generated Topic channel. Between her two versions the project rules and the evidence point the same way: the earlier EMI/Parsons (1965) beats the DG/Gage remake (1973/74, 4 stars, audibly forced high forte, made in her crisis window) - use ONLY the EMI/Parsons version. It also adds the dark dramatic-mezzo color the top-5 otherwise lacks next to soprano versions (Schwarzkopf et al.). Case against (why not 10): not the blind panel's winner, and one critical source (Gramophone) could not be consulted. Deducting one point for that; nothing else weighs against inclusion.

verified.singer: Lucia Popp (soprano, b. 12 Nov 1939 Záhorská Ves, d. 16 Nov 1993 Munich)
verified.pianist: Irwin Gage — CONFIRMED (Discogs release data and Warner Classics track credits both name Gage; producer John Mordler)
verified.recording_date: 1–6 November 1983, Abbey Road Studios, London (early digital recording); Gretchen is one of 16 songs from these sessions
verified.album_label: "Schubert: Lieder" — EMI / His Master's Voice Digital, released 1984 (German LP 1C 067 27 0067 1 / EL 27 0067 1; French La Voix de Son Maître 27 0067 1); Gretchen am Spinnrade D 118 is track 12 of 16
verified.reissues: EMI CD CDC 7 49633 2 (1984-era CD); track included on "The Very Best of Lucia Popp" (EMI, ℗1984 Parlophone credit; now distributed digitally by Warner Classics, Presto 5851022); the full 16-song recital also duplicated on CD7 of the Profil/Hänssler box "Queen of Night, Maiden of Light" (identical tracklist confirmed). IMPORTANT: this is Popp's ONLY documented commercial recording of D 118 — her Hyperion Schubert Edition Vol. 17 (April 1992, Graham Johnson) does NOT contain Gretchen; the Orfeo live Munich recital of 23 Jul 1984 with Gage (C789101) does not either; the Orfeo Salzburg 1981 recital with Parsons was a Slavic/Hungarian/German-late-Romantic programme. No earlier version exists to prefer.

age_voice: Popp was 43 (one week short of her 44th birthday, 12 Nov) at the sessions. Career arc (Wikipedia): coloratura/soubrette debut as Queen of the Night (1963), turned to lyric roles through the 1970s (Pamina, Sophie), and "by the 1980s when she was in her 40s and her voice matured further, she added more substantial roles" (Countess, Arabella, later the Marschallin). So Nov 1983 sits in her mature lyric mid-career — NOT a decline recording (she died at 54 with the voice still serviceable; her admired Hyperion Schubert disc came in 1992). However, retrospective critics note the trade-off: the famous silvery purity of the 1960s–70s had dimmed slightly, and her characteristic pulsing vibrato was more prominent — Tsaras London (2019): a "squeeze-box method of production, where each individual note is given a slight push which impedes the long legato line," and "the voice lost some of its silvery purity in the later recordings." Klassik-prisma hears at this exact recording an "unruhige, brüchige Stimme" (restless, brittle voice). Her timbre nonetheless remained convincingly youthful and bright — klassik-prisma's own essay names Popp (with Ziesak and Bonney) among singers who "können sehr glaubhaft mit jugendlichen hellen Stimmen aufwarten" (can very credibly offer youthful bright voices) for Gretchen.
reception: Popp's general standing as a Lieder singer is high and lasting (not PR): Gramophone called her Hyperion Schubert Vol. 17 "a moving and fitting memorial to one of the loveliest and most beloved singers." But for THIS Gretchen specifically, independent sources are consistently negative-to-lukewarm: (1) klassik-prisma.de's D 118 comparison table (verified directly from the page source) gives Popp/Gage/EMI/1983 (timed 3'36) the LOWEST grade in the survey, 3 on its 3-to-5 scale, with the verdict "unruhige, brüchige Stimme mit Problemen bei der deutschen Aussprache, lispelt" (restless, brittle voice with German-diction problems, lisps); its top grade 5 went to Schwarzkopf/E. Fischer 1952, Schwarzkopf/Parsons 1973, Ludwig/Parsons 1961, Janowitz/Gage 1977 and Zomer/Schoonderwoerd 2002. Note the head-to-head: the same pianist's Gretchen with Janowitz (DG 1977) rates 5, with Popp rates 3. (2) The Table d'écoute (RTBF) blind panel of 9 Aug 2020 did not include Popp among its compared versions (Norman, Ferrier, Ludwig, Fink, Janowitz, Schwarzkopf, Fleming) — an absence signal from a canon-forming exercise. (3) ClassicsToday (David Vernier) on "The Very Best of Lucia Popp": in the Schubert set she is "best in a rhythmically accented An Sylvia," and he faults the early-digital EMI sonics that "add base metal to Popp's silver." (4) Tsaras London retrospective (2019): "The Schubert songs expose a slight lack of colour," and she is "better at expressing joy, as in Die Forelle and An Sylvia, than the drama inherent in Gretchen am Spinnrade." The contemporary Gramophone review of the 1984 LP could not be retrieved (paywall/Cloudflare), so period-press verdicts are missing, but the retrospective consensus is clear: a lovely singer caught in a song that plays away from her strengths.

youtube.notes: Verified via oEmbed + page data: "Provided to YouTube by Warner Classics — Gretchen am Spinnrade, Op. 2, D. 118 · Lucia Popp · Irwin Gage — The Very Best of Lucia Popp — ℗ 1984 Parlophone Records Limited — Producer: John Mordler" — definitively THIS recording. Duration 3:44, uploaded 9 Feb 2017, ~16,600 views. Official Warner digital transfer; caveat: ClassicsToday found the compilation's transfers not freshly remastered, with early-digital glare.

"Lucia POPP sings Gretchen am Spinnrade", uploaded 6 Aug 2007, 3:45, ~222,000 views. Description gives no pianist/source; duration matches the EMI/Gage studio track so it is very likely the same recording, but unconfirmed; 2007-era upload implies low-bitrate audio. Prefer the Topic upload.
0:48 fragment only (paired with Camilla Horn film imagery) — an excerpt, not usable for the site.

concerns: 1) The contemporary Gramophone/period-press review of the 1984 LP was unreachable (Cloudflare/paywall; no Wayback snapshot), so reception rests on one German single-critic site (klassik-prisma), one retrospective blog (Tsaras London), and a ClassicsToday compilation review — directionally consistent, but thin. 2) Klassik-prisma's claim of "problems with German pronunciation / lisps" is surprising for Popp, who worked in Vienna/Munich for 30 years; treat that specific charge as one critic's ear, though the low grade itself is unambiguous (verified in the raw page source, not just a summary). 3) The high-view fan upload's source is unconfirmed (no pianist credit in description). 4) Early-digital EMI sound is itself a criticized element (glare/hardness) — a transfer-quality liability even in the official upload. 5) One WebFetch sub-summary falsely claimed Gretchen appears on Hyperion Vol. 17 and another invented a "Sawallisch 1984" Gretchen — both checked and refuted (Hyperion page itself says D 118 is absent; the Sawallisch album was R. Strauss); flagging so stray notes elsewhere don't resurrect them.
verdict: AGAINST top-5 inclusion — strength 3/10. Case for: Popp is a named priority singer; this is her ONLY recording of the song (so the "prefer earlier" rule is moot — nothing earlier exists); her timbre is genuinely, credibly girlish for Gretchen even at 43; and there is a clean official Topic-channel upload. Case against (decisive): the project's priority list is a proxy for quality, and on this specific song the independent evidence runs the other way — the klassik-prisma 28-version survey places this version at the very bottom of its scale (grade 3) while rule-favored competitors take the top grade (Schwarzkopf 1952 — the project's #1 woman, Ludwig 1961, Janowitz 1977 with the very same pianist); the 2020 blind panel ignored it; retrospective critics find her short on the song's drama and colour ("better at expressing joy... than the drama inherent in Gretchen am Spinnrade"). The D 118 field is among the deepest in the Lied catalogue (Schumann, Lehmann, Ferrier, Schwarzkopf, Seefried, Ludwig, Baker, Janowitz all available), so a version whose only claim is the singer's name, not this performance's standing, does not merit one of five slots. Recommend instead: keep Popp in reserve as a stylistic-contrast alternate (bright youthful voice, modern stereo, official upload) if a chosen candidate fails YouTube-availability checks, and channel the Popp priority toward songs that suit her (An Silvia, Die Forelle, Seligkeit — from these same 1983 sessions — where even her critics concede she excels).

verified.singer: Gundula Janowitz, soprano (b. 2 Aug 1937, Berlin; Austrian, raised in Graz)
verified.recording_date: Berlin, Studio Lankwitz; sessions 9-10/1976 and 9 & 12/1977 (per DG reissue booklet notes quoted on Discogs r7236950). Gretchen D 118 carries P-1978 (not in the P-1977 track group), so most likely Sept or Dec 1977?; klassik-prisma dates the version 1977. Exact session day unverifiable from public sources.
verified.album_label: First issued in the 5-LP box 'Lieder (Volume I)', Deutsche Grammophon 2740 196 (1978), side B tr. 3, 3:57 (Discogs r12034254). Engineers Karl-August Naegler / Wolfgang Mitlehner, producer Cord Garben. Note: the associated single-LP recital DG 2530 858 (1977, Deutscher Schallplattenpreis) from the same sessions does NOT contain Gretchen — the box does. The set is 5 LPs on Discogs, not 4 as the task stated (the complete sessions fill 4 CDs in the 2017 Edition, likely the source of the '4' figure).
verified.reissues: 2-CD DG 453 082-2 'Lieder' (1997, Original-Image Bit-Processing remaster; Gretchen tr. 1-2, 4:04) and companion 453 139-2 'Lieder (Volume 2)' (1998); 'The Gundula Janowitz Edition' 14-CD box (DG, 2017, for her 80th birthday — the Schubert/Gage recordings occupy CDs 10-13); in the streaming catalogue via UMG (source of the YouTube Topic upload, whose metadata gives 'The Gundula Janowitz Edition', 1978).

age_voice: Janowitz was 39 at the 1976 sessions, 40 at the Sept/Dec 1977 ones. This sits at the late plateau of her prime, not past it: her benchmark Karajan Four Last Songs (rec. 1972-73) is press-described as made "in her vocal prime" and Gramophone still calls it unsurpassed "for Straussian opulence and tenderness"; Wikipedia dates her pre-eminence to "the 1960s and 1970s", with an unusually durable career (opera to 1990, recitals into the late 90s). Direct contemporary evidence for these very sessions: Eric Sams's Gramophone review (Nov 1977, p. 874, of the first LP from the sessions) reports no wear — "her warmth of tone and diction make it flower most attractively" — while noting she "emphasizes melodic rather than verbal expressiveness", the standard caveat about her Lieder singing (glorious instrument, generalized word-treatment). No reviewer I found describes any vocal decline in this set; audible decline in her case is usually located in the mid-1980s. This is also her only studio Gretchen, so the project's "earlier recording of the same singer wins" rule has no competing earlier studio version.
reception: Lasting, independent standing rather than PR: (1) klassik-prisma.de's 28-version comparison (compiled 2003, upd. 2009) gives Janowitz/Gage (DGG, 1977, 3'57) 5 stars — one of only five top ratings, alongside Schwarzkopf/Fischer 1952, Schwarzkopf/Parsons 1973, the young Ludwig's EMI version, and Zomer/Schoonderwoerd. Important nuance I verified in the German text: the famous praise of Gage — "Von allen beteiligten Klavierbegleitern spielt sich Irwin Gage an die Spitze; bei ihm hört man... dass Schubert den Klavierpart 3-stimmig angelegt hat... Gage gelingt diese Stelle meisterhaft!" — declares him the best accompanist of the entire survey but appears in the Christa Ludwig paragraph (Ludwig also recorded the song with Gage later, a version the site criticizes); the Janowitz entry itself is a wordless 5-star table row. (2) Contemporary: Sams's positive Gramophone review Nov 1977; the series won the Deutscher Schallplattenpreis (sticker on DG 2530 858, Discogs). (3) The set has never left the DG catalogue (1997/1998 CDs, 2017 Edition) — the project's research file calls it "one of the most admired Schubert recital sets of the LP era". (4) Counter-evidence, honestly: the RTBF 'table d'écoute' blind panel (post of 1 Mar 2020, tablecoute.blogspot.com) included Janowitz/Gage as Version E of 8 but chose Fink/Huber and Schwarzkopf/Fischer (the post lists versions and winners only, no per-version commentary); and Gramophone's current '50 greatest Schubert recordings' represents Janowitz not by this studio set but by her live 1972 Salzburg recital with Gage (Orfeo C592021), praising "a soprano often mistakenly considered no more than a singer with a lovely voice". Net: canonical top-tier version by durable critical consensus, but not the unanimous first choice — that remains Schwarzkopf/Fischer.

youtube.notes: Title 'Schubert: Gretchen am Spinnrade, D. 118'; UMG-provided auto-generated upload, metadata sourced from 'The Gundula Janowitz Edition' (DG remaster lineage, 1997 Original-Image Bit-Processing/2017 Edition; digital year shown as 1978 = P-year). oEmbed returns an embed iframe, so embedding is enabled. Best link for the site.

Title 'Gretchen am Spinnrade - Schubert (Gundula Janowitz - Soprano)'; presumed transfer of this DG studio recording but the source pressing and identity are not audio-verified; link-rot and takedown risk higher than Topic upload.
Title 'Gundula Janowitz: Gretchen am Spinnrade by Schubert'; same caveat — not audio-verified as this exact studio take (Janowitz also has live material in circulation).

concerns: 1) Exact session date for Gretchen unpinned — somewhere in 9-10/1976 or 9/12 1977; P-1978. 2) The task's premise slightly overstates klassik-prisma: the Gage spinning-figuration praise is written in the Ludwig section (about his playing generally/in the later Ludwig version), not as prose on the Janowitz entry — the Janowitz 5-star rating stands, but the site publishes no words about her singing here, so we cannot quote it in her support. 3) The '4-LP set' description is wrong per Discogs (5-LP box 2740 196); use correct data on the site. 4) The 2020 blind panel passed her over for Fink and Schwarzkopf, and Gramophone's 50-greatest prefers her 1972 Salzburg live recital — I could not verify whether that 1972 program even included Gretchen, so no earlier Janowitz version of this song is confirmed to exist. 5) Fan uploads not audio-verified against the studio take. 6) Topic-upload region-blocking cannot be tested from this environment; embed works per oEmbed but per-territory licensing may differ. 7) Recurring critical caveat (Sams): line over word — in a dramatic scena like Gretchen some listeners find her too instrumental; klassik-prisma's own prose argues the song must be acted as a scene, yet still rated her 5 stars.
verdict: FOR: a golden-age (b. 1937) singer recorded at 39-40 in still-prime voice, from one of the LP era's most admired Schubert recital sets (Schallplattenpreis series, never out of the DG catalogue); one of only five 5-star versions in the deepest independent comparison (klassik-prisma, 28 versions); accompanist rated the best in that survey; official embeddable Topic upload of a modern DG remaster exists. It is the natural 'radiantly beautiful lyric soprano' slot beside the more word-driven Schwarzkopf and Ludwig, giving the top-5 timbral and interpretive variety. AGAINST: not on the project's named priority list; lost the 2020 blind panel to Schwarzkopf/Fischer and Fink; the specific Gage praise often cited for it belongs textually to the Ludwig discussion; as a mid-70s stereo studio product it is neither a historic document nor a period-instrument outlier. Under the project's rules (old masters first, verified vocal condition, skepticism toward hype — none of which count against a 1977 recording with 45+ years of sustained standing), this is a strong, safe top-5 member but not the No. 1, which should remain Schwarzkopf/Fischer 1952. Recommended placement: slot 2-4. Strength: 8/10.

verified.singer: Lotte Lehmann (soprano, 1888-1976) — her ONLY studio recording of D 118 (confirmed by searching the complete Lotte Lehmann League discography: no Odeon-era or 1940s Columbia/RCA remake exists)
verified.recording_date: 16 March 1937 (Lotte Lehmann League discography entry 274; matrix BS 06664-1, with a note 'J.: adds 1A' — a second take documented in one source)
verified.album_label: RCA Victor 1856 (10" 78) / HMV DA 1603; also included in Victor album M-419
verified.reissues: Romophone 81013-2 'The Victor Recordings 1935-1940' (Obert-Thorn transfers; reviewed Gramophone 5/1996); Naxos Historical 8.111093 'Lieder Recordings Vol. 1 (1935-1937)' (2006, track 29, Mark Obert-Thorn restoration); 'Schubert: Lieder (Les Indispensables de Diapason)' compilation (2023, via IDOL)

age_voice: She was 49 (b. 27 Feb 1888, Perleberg) — past her 1920s Vienna operatic prime (she left Vienna in 1938, dropped heavier roles through the 1940s, farewell recital 1951), but squarely inside what critics treat as her LIEDER prime: the Salzburg Liederabende with Bruno Walter became an institution from 1934, and the 1935-40 Victor series is her core song legacy. Alan Blyth's independent Gramophone review (5/1996) of this exact series: "Lotte Lehmann was at the height of her powers as a song interpreter in the late 1930s: the bloom of youth is still in the tone, now enhanced by the experience of many years of stage interpretation." The Lotte Lehmann League's comparison page likewise calls a 1935 studio recording from this series "her in her prime." Standard caveats about Lehmann (short breath spans, phrases broken early) predate 1937 and were lifelong traits, not signs of decline at this session. Net: interpretively at peak, vocally late-bloom but not yet in decline — clearly preferable to her 1941-49 recordings, and no earlier alternative exists.
reception: Strong lasting reputation from independent retrospective criticism, not PR. Alan Blyth (Gramophone 5/1996, Romophone reissue review — recovered via Wayback Machine) singles out THIS track: "Her impassioned Gretchen in Schubert's great song is sister to, and inhabits the same world as, Lehmann's Leonore and Sieglinde," praising readings that are "generous and free, never dull... [not] overladen with detailed word-painting in the Schwarzkopf manner." A 2023 French critical-anthology endorsement: Diapason chose this recording for its curated 'Les Indispensables de Diapason' Schubert Lieder set. IMPORTANT NEGATIVES: the recording is absent from both project anchor comparisons — klassik-prisma.de's 28-version survey (its 5 stars go to Schwarzkopf/Fischer 1952, Schwarzkopf/Parsons 1973, Ludwig/Parsons 1961, Janowitz/Gage 1977, Zomer/Schoonderwoerd) and the tablecoute.blogspot.com March 2020 blind panel (8 versions: Norman, Ferrier, Ludwig, Fink, Janowitz, Schwarzkopf, Fleming, Dessay; winners Schwarzkopf/Fischer and Fink/Huber). So there is no head-to-head comparative verdict; its standing rests on Lehmann's canonical stature and Blyth's specific praise. The Naxos liner claim of 'no audible decline' in her 1937 sessions is label text and was discounted per project rules — but Blyth's independent judgment points the same way.

youtube.notes: Description verified: 'Provided to YouTube by NAXOS of America... Lehmann, Lotte: Lieder Recordings, Vol. 1 (1935-1937), ℗ 2006 Naxos, Artist: Erno Balogh' — i.e., the Mark Obert-Thorn restoration, the best available transfer. Duration 3:41, published 10 Aug 2018, ~810 views. playabilityStatus OK, playableInEmbed true (checked).

Description verified: 'Provided to YouTube by IDOL... Schubert: Lieder (Les indispensables de Diapason), ℗ Reworld Media, Piano: Ernő Balogh.' Duration 3:40, published 11 Apr 2024, ~130 views. Good backup with independent (Diapason-sourced) remastering. Embeddable, playability OK (checked).

Title 'Lotte Lehmann sings Gretchen am Spinnrade', uploaded 26 Feb 2011, ~1350 views, duration 3:50 — 9s longer than the Topic uploads, suggesting a slower/lower-pitched 78 transfer or lead-in silence; no description/provenance. Embeddable but least preferred.

concerns: 1) No head-to-head data: excluded from both klassik-prisma's 28-version comparison and the tablecoute 2020 blind panel, so its rank against Schwarzkopf/Fischer or Ludwig is inference, not measured consensus. 2) 1937 78rpm mono: surface noise, boxy piano; even Blyth noted the Romophone digitization "imparted a slight glare" to her tone — the Naxos/Obert-Thorn transfer on the Topic upload is the safest choice. 3) The fan upload's 3:50 duration raises a pitch/speed question; use the Topic upload. 4) Naxos Historical CDs are not sold in the US for copyright reasons; the Naxos Topic upload played and embedded fine from this environment, but region-blocking elsewhere cannot be fully ruled out — the 2023 IDOL/Diapason Topic upload is a hedge. 5) Discography notes a take 1A besides BS 06664-1; which take underlies each transfer is undocumented (minor). 6) I could not access Gramophone's contemporary 1937/38 review of HMV DA 1603 (archive paywalled); reception evidence is retrospective.
verdict: INCLUDE — strength 8/10. Under the project rules this is close to an ideal old-master pick: a canonical pre-war Schubertian (first woman to record Winterreise) in her ONLY studio Gretchen, made at her interpretive peak with independent retrospective authority (Alan Blyth, Gramophone) praising this exact track as operatic-scale Gretchen singing, plus a 2023 Diapason anthology endorsement — lasting reputation, not label PR. It is the earliest strong-provenance Gretchen with a label-sourced YouTube transfer, predating Elisabeth Schumann/Moore (1945), Ferrier (1947) and Schwarzkopf/Fischer (1952), and no earlier Lehmann version exists to prefer. Docked two points because it sits outside both anchor comparison surveys (so no measured consensus placing it above the Schwarzkopf/Ludwig tier) and because 1937 sonics will be the harshest of any top-5 candidate. Sensible placement: the pre-war old-master slot, ranked below Schwarzkopf/Fischer 1952 but above modern versions; recommended video HCKNyg5E5J4 (Naxos/Obert-Thorn, Topic channel).

verified.singer: Elisabeth Schwarzkopf, soprano (b. 9 Dec 1915 - d. 3 Aug 2006)
verified.recording_date: 4-7 October 1952, EMI Abbey Road Studio No. 1A, London; producer Walter Legge (Legge credit verified from Warner Classics metadata on the official Topic upload; dates/studio verified via MusicWeb review of Naxos 8.111287 and the davidhertzberg upload notes)
verified.album_label: Columbia (EMI) Schubert song recital LP, 33CX 1040, released 1953 (catalogue number confirmed via multiple dealer listings; 12 Schubert songs from the Fischer sessions incl. Gretchen am Spinnrade D 118)
verified.reissues: EMI/Warner 'Schubert: Lieder' - Warner metadata reads 'P 1953, 2000 Parlophone Records Limited' (the 2000 EMI remaster now under Warner, streaming/YouTube); Naxos Historical 8.111287 'Schubert: Lieder (Schwarzkopf) (1952-1954)' (2008; Gretchen is track 6, 3:24; not distributed in the US per Naxos site); Musical Concepts/Alto 'The Best of Elisabeth Schwarzkopf' (P 2012); a competing Urania edition also noted by MusicWeb. Exact EMI References/GROC CD catalogue numbers not verifiable this session (Discogs/Presto/Gramophone all returned 403).

age_voice: Schwarzkopf was 36 (two months short of 37) at the October 1952 sessions - squarely within her vocal prime (generally placed late 1940s to late 1950s). Naxos's liner blurb says the set captures her "in her absolute prime"; that is label copy, but it is independently corroborated: MusicWeb's 2008 reviewer (Goran Forsling) wrote that "rarely if ever has Elisabeth Schwarzkopf sounded better or given so lovely and unaffected readings of German Lieder" - significant wording, since the standard criticism of later Schwarzkopf is over-inflected mannerism; the 1952 recital is prized precisely for its relative directness. Fischer, 66 and near the end of his career, is credited by the same review as the catalyst who "managed to invest the piano part with that little extra that becomes the germ for great music-making." By contrast, at the 1973 remake with Geoffrey Parsons she was 57, and even the admiring klassik-prisma reviewer concedes the listener "must accept some vocal discolorations" (Vokalverfaerbungen) there.
reception: Lasting reputation, not PR: (1) klassik-prisma.de's comparative survey of Gretchen am Spinnrade - 31 versions as currently posted (the project brief's "28" appears to reflect an earlier page state) - gives 5 stars to only five versions, including Schwarzkopf/Fischer 1952; the reviewer rates her 1952 and 1973 versions "ziemlich ebenbuertig" (roughly equal), noting only that the 1952 sound is "zeitbedingt etwas stumpf" (period-typical, somewhat dull). (2) tablecoute.blogspot.com's blind listening session of 1 March 2020 pitted 8 versions (Norman/Moll, Ferrier/Spurr, Ludwig/Parsons, Fink/Huber, Janowitz/Gage, Schwarzkopf/Fischer, Fleming/Eschenbach, Dessay/Cassard) and the Schwarzkopf/Fischer recording emerged as the panel's preferred version. (3) MusicWeb International (Oct 2008, on Naxos 8.111287): Schwarzkopf "rarely if ever... sounded better," Fischer singled out as the session's inspirational core, transfer "more than acceptable" and superior in presentation to the Urania rival. (4) Structural evidence of standing: continuous reissue for 70+ years across Columbia LP, EMI remaster (2000), Naxos Historical, and licensed compilations - the recital predates the modern press-PR machine entirely, so its reputation is organically accumulated. Caveat: I could not reach the Gramophone archive (403) to quote period or retrospective Gramophone reviews directly.

youtube.notes: BEST CHOICE. 'Provided to YouTube by Warner Classics', album 'Schubert: Lieder', P-line 'P 1953, 2000 Parlophone Records Limited' - i.e. the rights-holder's 2000 EMI remaster. Credits Piano: Edwin Fischer, Soprano: Elisabeth Schwarzkopf, Producer: Walter Legge. Duration 3:29 (209 s), 1,116 views at check (2026-08-14). Official-catalogue audio, cleanest provenance.

Well-documented fan upload (27 Jul 2020, 5,557 views, 3:25/205 s); description correctly states 'Recorded October 4-7, 1952 at No. 1A Studio, Abbey Road, London' and includes full text. Transfer source unstated. Good fallback with the most watch-history.

'Provided to YouTube by Musical Concepts' from 'The Best of Elisabeth Schwarzkopf' (P 2012, Alto/Musical Concepts licensed compilation). 3:18 (198 s - trimmed lead-in/out), uploaded 11 Mar 2025, only 48 views. Legitimate but a budget-label transfer; prefer the Warner Topic upload.
Fan upload, 3:27 (207 s), 111 views, empty description - same 1952 recording per title but no sourcing info. Lowest priority.

CAUTION - DIFFERENT RECORDING: this is the live Turin 1954 radio recording with Fischer (3:39/219 s, 14,091 views). Listed here only so it is not mistaken for the 1952 studio version; off-air sound, later date - the rules favor the studio 1952.

concerns: (1) The session's WebSearch budget was exhausted before this task started; all research was done via WebFetch and curl. Gramophone archive, Discogs, and Presto returned 403, so I could not verify original 1953 Gramophone reviews or exact EMI References/GROC CD catalogue numbers - the reissue chain is reconstructed from Naxos, MusicWeb, dealer listings, and Warner's own YouTube metadata. (2) tablecoute: the fetched page text lists the 8 versions and shows Schwarzkopf/Fischer as the retained/preferred version, but the panel's scoring detail (and whether the win was 'joint', as the project brief states) was not extractable from the page - the detail may live in the embedded radio broadcast. The blog also dates the recording 1953 (LP release year), a harmless discrepancy. (3) klassik-prisma now counts 31 versions, not 28, and rates the 1952 and 1973 Schwarzkopf versions as near-equal - so that source alone does not decide between her versions; the project's age rule does. (4) Attribution risk is very low: the Warner Topic upload carries full artist/producer credits, and Fischer recorded this song with her only in the 1952 studio sessions (plus the Turin live, clearly labeled); durations 3:18-3:29 across uploads are consistent with trim differences, though I could not audio-verify the uploads or check region-availability/embed status of the Topic uploads from page JSON alone. (5) Sound is 1952 mono, described by klassik-prisma as somewhat dull ('zeitbedingt etwas stumpf') - fine for a historical pick but worth a line on the site. (6) View counts/durations were read on 2026-08-14 and will drift.
verdict: STRONG INCLUDE - strength 10/10. This is the project's paradigm case: the #1 priority female singer, aged 36 and by independent testimony at or near her absolute vocal peak, partnered by a legendary Schubertian pianist, produced by Walter Legge, in a recording whose top standing is confirmed by every independent source consulted (5 stars in klassik-prisma's 31-version survey; the 2020 tablecoute blind panel's preferred version against Ferrier, Ludwig, Janowitz, Norman, Fleming; MusicWeb: 'rarely if ever has Schwarzkopf sounded better') and by 70+ years of continuous reissue - reputation earned long before modern PR. Among her own three versions the project rules point unambiguously here: earlier beats later (1952 studio vs Turin live 1954 vs the 1973 Parsons remake, where even a 5-star reviewer concedes vocal discoloration at age 57), and the 1952 has studio sound the Turin off-air tape lacks. Recommended upload: the Warner Classics Topic video (6-RjxuXSuPw, 2000 Parlophone remaster), with the davidhertzberg fan transfer as fallback. If the top-5 needs only one Schwarzkopf Gretchen, it is this one.

verified.singer: Irmgard Seefried, soprano (b. 9 Oct 1919, Köngetried — d. 24 Nov 1988)
verified.pianist: Erik Werba (her regular accompanist through the 1950s-60s)
verified.recording_date: 7–9 October 1957, Brahms-Saal, Musikverein, Vienna (producer Hans Ritter, engineer Heinz Wildhagen; ℗ 1957 DG). NOT 1956 — the fan upload's '1956' title is wrong. The '1962' found in some sources is a SECOND, separate DG studio remake: 5–8 February 1962, same hall, producer Hans Weber, engineer Gerhard Henjes (timing ~3:26 vs 3:36). So she recorded the song TWICE for DG; this candidate is the earlier 1957 version.
verified.album_label: Deutsche Grammophon recording, first confirmed issue in the US as Decca DL 9974 (1958) — per the uploader's LP documentation; European DG first issue of the 1957 take not pinned down (the Gretchen on DG 136 372 SLPEM 'Lieder von Schubert, Schumann, Brahms', 9/1962 stereo, is the 1962 remake, confirmed by ℗1962 credits and timings)
verified.reissues: First CD release only in Eloquence 'The Art of Irmgard Seefried' Vol. 4 (DG/Eloquence, notes by Richard Wigmore; digital album 'Schubert: Lieder' DG 484 3274). The 1962 remake is on Eloquence Vol. 5 (tracks 19–22: Goethe/Faust group). Gray-market copies of the 1962 LP exist via BNF Collection/The Restoration Project (Believe SAS).

age_voice: Sessions straddled her 38th birthday (7–9 Oct 1957; born 9 Oct 1919). Consensus biography (AllMusic): in the 1940s–early 1950s she was 'a paragon among German lyric sopranos, her voice fresh and crystalline'; 'by the late 1950s, an early decline, which some have attributed to singing too late into pregnancy and returning to the stage too soon after childbirth, stole a good measure of freedom from her singing although she remained a strong artist dramatically.' So Oct 1957 sits at the tail end of her good years — slightly past absolute bloom, clearly better preserved than her 1962/1968 versions. The contemporary Gramophone review quoted on the Eloquence Vol. 4 page supports this: 'the quality of the voice, the balance and the piano tone are of amazing fidelity. Interpretatively too, Mme Seefried is at her most penetrating and revealing, scrupulous with words and their meaning... immensely vital in rhythm.' This is the EARLIEST of her five-plus known Gretchen recordings (DG studio Oct 1957; Salzburg live 1957/Orfeo; BBC live 1962; DG studio remake Feb 1962; Ades 1968), so under the project's earlier-wins rule it is the correct Seefried version to consider.
reception: Her overall lieder standing is lasting and independent of PR: Alan Blyth (Gramophone): 'If I were condemned to hear only one voice for the remainder of my life I think it might well be hers'; Schwarzkopf herself said all colleagues envied how naturally she sang 'from the heart' (both quoted by Eloquence). Period Gramophone criticism of these DG sessions was enthusiastic (quote above — that is 1950s-era criticism, not modern label PR). HOWEVER, for this exact version the comparative record is thin: klassik-prisma's 30-version Gretchen comparison (checked in full from a saved copy) does NOT include the 1957 DG studio recording at all — it rates her Orfeo 1957 live 4, BBC 1962 live 4–5, and 'Ades 1968' 4–5 (that Ades entry, at 3'16, may actually be the 1962 DG remake, ~3:26 with tail silence, in French reissue clothing — unresolved), with only mild criticisms (shortened 'ge-' in 'vergehen', lengthened s in 'Kuss'). Its top tier (grade 5) is Schwarzkopf 1952 & 1973, Ludwig 1961, Janowitz 1977, Zomer 2002 — Seefried lands a tier below. The tablecoute.blogspot March 2020 blind panel on D 118 (saved copy checked) did not include Seefried at all. The Eloquence-era reissue reviews praise the series but are partly promotional; I weighted the period Gramophone text and klassik-prisma grades over those.

youtube.notes: THE 1957 studio recording: 'Provided to YouTube by Universal Music Group... The Art of Irmgard Seefried... ℗ 1957 Deutsche Grammophon GmbH, Berlin... Producer: Hans Ritter, Balance Engineer: Heinz Wildhagen'. Duration 3:36 (216 s), uploaded 2021-01-15, 132 views. WARNING: the watch page returned playabilityStatus UNPLAYABLE / 'Video unavailable' from my US test location — region-blocked or withdrawn; must be re-verified in the target region before embedding.

Playable and embeddable (status OK, playableInEmbed true). Transfer of the US Decca DL 9974 LP (1958 pressing); title mis-dates it '1956' — same DG Oct 1957 recording per ℗1957 metadata and the uploader's own Ganymed companion video ('issued in 1958... DL 9974'). 3:45 (incl. LP lead-in/out; slightly longer than official 3:36 — possible marginally slow transfer, not audibly verified). Uploaded 2021-11-09, 531 views; uploader documents a serious transfer chain (Technics SL1200MK5, AT95e, RDL phono pre, Scarlett 2i2) on his related uploads.

NOT the candidate — this is the Feb 1962 DG stereo REMAKE ('The Art Of Irmgard Seefried – Volume 5', ℗ 1962 DG, producer Hans Weber, engineer Gerhard Henjes), 3:26, playable and embeddable. Listed here to prevent mix-ups; per project rules the 1957 version outranks it.

concerns: 1) Two premise errors in the brief: the date is Oct 1957 (not ~1956), and klassik-prisma does NOT rate this recording — it rates three OTHER Seefried versions 4 to 4–5; this exact version has essentially no independent comparative ranking (also absent from the tablecoute 2020 blind panel). 2) High mix-up risk: two DG studio versions (1957 mono-era and 1962 stereo remake) circulate under near-identical titling on YouTube/streaming; the only clean playable Topic upload is of the WRONG (1962) version. 3) The official Topic upload of the 1957 version was unplayable ('Video unavailable') from my test location — unverified whether it plays in the site's target regions. 4) The playable 1957 option is a fan LP transfer with an erroneous '1956' in its title and a ~4% longer duration than the official file (lead-in silence or slightly slow pitch — not audibly verified as the identical take, though ℗ metadata makes it near-certain). 5) European first issue of the 1957 take not pinned down; DL 9974's full tracklist unverified (Discogs blocked direct fetch). 6) The identity of klassik-prisma's 'Ades 1968' entry (possibly the 1962 DG remake) is unresolved.
verdict: FOR: genuine old-master credentials (golden-age Vienna soprano, Werba at the piano, recorded 1957); her earliest Gretchen, made just at the edge of her prime at age 38, before the documented late-50s decline; period Gramophone praise ('at her most penetrating and revealing') rather than modern PR; a beloved, natural Schubertian by lasting critical consensus (Blyth, Steane, Schwarzkopf's tribute). AGAINST: this exact version is absent from both independent comparisons the project leans on, and where Seefried's Gretchen IS rated (klassik-prisma) she sits a tier (4 to 4–5) below the 5-rated Schwarzkopf 1952/1973 and Ludwig 1961 — two singers already above her on the project's priority list, alongside E. Schumann and Popp; and the YouTube situation for the 1957 version is weak (official upload unplayable from test location; playable copy is a mis-dated fan transfer). Verdict: a defensible slot-4/slot-5 candidate if the curators want Seefried's old-Vienna voice represented and can either confirm the Topic upload plays for their audience or accept the fan transfer — but not a lock against Schwarzkopf '52, Elisabeth Schumann, or young Ludwig. Strength: 5/10.

verified.pianist: Phyllis Spurr (Decca house accompanist; some reissues misspell 'Phylis Spur')
verified.recording_date: 14 March 1947, Decca studios, Broadhurst Gardens, West Hampstead, London (per Wikipedia 'Kathleen Ferrier discography'); same session produced Die junge Nonne D 828. Her only studio Gretchen — so attribution of any reissue is unambiguous. One fan upload is titled '1946' — that date is wrong.
verified.album_label: Original issue: Decca 78 rpm, 12", cat. K1632, coupling Gretchen am Spinnrade / Die junge Nonne (confirmed by 401dutchdivas.nl discography and Discogs release 11106813, shellac 12" 78 rpm). ℗ 1947 Decca Music Group Limited.
verified.reissues: US London label LP (late 1950s); Kathleen Ferrier Edition Vol. 4 'Schumann/Schubert/Brahms' (Decca 433 471-2, the source of the current UMG streaming/YouTube track, ~3:14); Kathleen Ferrier Centenary Edition — The Complete Decca Recordings (Decca, 2012); Naxos Historical 8.112071 'Vocal Recital 1946–1950' (track 15); Regis 'What Is Life?' (2010); gray-label transfers: Urania (2006), Phonogold 'Songs 1912–1953' (2016).

age_voice: Ferrier was 34 (born 22 April 1912) — chronologically early but in the fresh full bloom of a career that lasted only ~10 years. Context: professional career from ~1943; created Britten's Lucretia at Glyndebourne 1946; moved from Columbia to Decca after friction with Walter Legge; her transformative mentorship with Bruno Walter ("one of the greatest singers of our time") began only at the September 1947 Edinburgh Festival — i.e., this Gretchen PREDATES the Walter partnership that shaped her mature lieder style. Her celebrated lieder documents (1949 Edinburgh recital with Walter, 1952 Das Lied) all come later. So the voice itself is at or near its peak — no late-career decline issue (she died in 1953; decline only set in with illness from late 1952) — but interpretive/idiomatic maturity is pre-prime. This matches klassik-prisma's verdict on this disc: "gebremste Emotionen" (reined-in emotions). On German diction the evidence is mixed: MusicWeb's Christopher Fifield, reviewing the compilation containing these sides, wrote "In Lieder her German is excellent, especially in Schubert's songs accompanied sensitively by Phyllis Spurr" — so the frequent claim that her early German was weak is not supported by the independent review found; but no contemporary 1947 Gramophone review could be accessed to confirm period reception.
reception: Lasting reputation, not PR: Ferrier is a canonical old master with a genuine posthumous cult, and this Decca side has stayed continuously in print for ~79 years. But independent comparative sources place THIS recording below the song's benchmark tier: (1) klassik-prisma.de's 28-version survey (1926–2007) gives it 4 of 5 stars with the terse comment "gebremste Emotionen, Rauschen der Schellackplatte" (restrained emotions, shellac surface noise), while 5 stars went to Schwarzkopf/Fischer 1952, Schwarzkopf/Parsons 1973, Ludwig/Parsons, Janowitz/Gage 1977 and Zomer/Schoonderwoerd 2002. (2) The March 2020 tablecoute.blogspot.com blind panel included it as Version B among 8 versions; the winners were Fink/Huber 2008 and Schwarzkopf/Fischer — Ferrier did not win, though a listener memorably called her reading "comme une confession chuchotée" (like a whispered confession). (3) MusicWeb reviewers of the compilation are warm but general: John Quinn — "the quality of the voice and the conviction of the singing overcome any such quibbles"; Fifield praises her German and Spurr's sensitivity. The low-voice reading: critics treat it as an introspective, inward Gretchen — the whispered-confession quality is its distinction — rather than the surging dramatic soprano scena; the 4-star rating and "restrained emotions" comment indicate the climaxes ('Sein Kuss!') are where it yields to Schwarzkopf and Ludwig. At ~3:14 it is also one of the fastest versions on record (78-side economics likely a factor).

'Schubert: Gretchen am Spinnrade, D.118', 3:14, 'Provided to YouTube by Universal Music Group', album 'Kathleen Ferrier Vol. 4 - Schumann / Schubert / Brahms', ℗ 1947 Decca Music Group Limited — i.e. Decca's own official transfer (Kathleen Ferrier Edition). Verified by parsing the watch page. Low views (732) but that is normal for Topic duplicates.
Same recording via The Orchard / Regis Records 2010 compilation 'What Is Life?', 3:10, 2,564 views. Gray-label transfer — usable backup, but the UMG/Decca one above is preferable.
Phonogold 'Songs 1912-1953' (2016) transfer, 3:12. Gray label; backup only.
3:11, correctly attributed to Ferrier/Spurr in the title; duration matches the official track, so almost certainly the same 1947 recording.

The upload cited in the project's research file. Verified: 'Schubert / Kathleen Ferrier, 1946: Gretchen am Spinnrade - London LP', uploaded 18 Dec 2015, 5,684 views, digitized from a late-1950s US London (=Decca) LP. Two red flags: title says '1946' (wrong — session was 14 Mar 1947) and duration is 5:50 vs the official 3:14, suggesting a wrong-speed transfer or appended material. Do NOT use as the primary link; replace with the Topic/UMG upload.

concerns: 1) Could not access the Gramophone archive or Paul Campion's 'Ferrier: A Career Recorded' (the authoritative session discography), so the matrix number and the contemporary 1947-48 press reception are unverified; the 14 Mar 1947 date rests on Wikipedia's discography (which is sourced to Campion). 2) The performing key is unverified — as a contralto she almost certainly sang it transposed down from the original D minor, but no source explicitly confirming the key was found; worth checking before writing site copy. 3) The currently noted fan upload (1DgOGtakngQ) is mislabeled '1946' and runs 5:50 — an anomalous duration that suggests a defective (slow) transfer; the project file should be corrected to the Topic/UMG upload. 4) Topic uploads are auto-generated and occasionally region-restricted or non-embeddable; embeddability was not testable from this sandbox. 5) The klassik-prisma comment is only six words — thin evidence, though its 4-star (not 5-star) placement is unambiguous. 6) 'Grokipedia' praise found in search results is AI-generated and was disregarded.
verdict: CASE FOR: a true old master (canonical status, not PR — reputation sustained 70+ years), her ONLY studio Gretchen so no earlier-version conflict, voice in fresh bloom at 34, pre-1950 historic weight, a distinctive inward 'whispered confession' contralto reading that diversifies a top-5 otherwise dominated by sopranos/mezzos, and a verified official Decca transfer on a Topic channel. CASE AGAINST: in both independent comparisons this version sits below the benchmark tier — 4/5 stars at klassik-prisma (vs five 5-star versions led by Schwarzkopf/Fischer) and a non-winner in the 2020 blind panel; the reading is emotionally reined-in and very fast (~3:14), made before Bruno Walter shaped her lieder art; shellac noise is audible; and for the 'historic old-master' slot she competes directly with Elisabeth Schumann (a named project priority) and Lotte Lehmann. Verdict: a legitimate, defensible candidate for slot 4-5 as the historic contralto counterweight — clearly behind Schwarzkopf/Fischer 1952 and Ludwig, roughly level with the other historic ladies on merit but ahead of them in name recognition and YouTube availability. Strength: 6/10.

A physical HM Gold (HMG 501991-type) reissue could NOT be verified — searches surfaced only the original HMC 901991.

age_voice: Fink was 52 at the September 2007 sessions — late in her career (began mid-1980s, European prime from the 1990s Jacobs/Harnoncourt Baroque years through her 2000s harmonia mundi Lieder series) but demonstrably at the late edge of her prime, not past it. Contemporary reviews describe the voice as fresh: BBC Music Magazine (Oct 2008) called it a 'clear, unfettered lyrical mezzo'; the Sunday Telegraph heard 'no arch mannerisms, no exaggerated emotion, but no lack of passion and insight'; audaud.com said she was 'rapidly ascending to one of the finest mezzo-sopranos in the world today'; klassik-prisma.de even likens the timbre to Irmgard Seefried's — i.e. lighter and more girlish than the typical 52-year-old mezzo, which matters for a 16-year-old Gretchen. The only vocal (as opposed to interpretive) criticism found is OpusKlassiek's complaint that her vibrato 'often compromises the purity' the song demands. So: no evidence of vocal decline at this recording; criticisms target interpretation, not vocal estate. This is also her only commercial Gretchen, so no earlier-version-of-same-singer rule applies.
reception: Genuinely mixed-to-strong, and the strongest credential is independent, not PR. (1) The table d'ecoute blind panel (RTBF Musiq3, broadcast 1 March 2020, blog tablecoute.blogspot.com): eight versions blind-compared (Norman, Ferrier, Ludwig/Parsons, Fink/Huber, Janowitz/Gage, Schwarzkopf/Fischer, Fleming, Dessay); verbatim verdict 'Version choisie Gretchen am Spinnrade : D & F' — Fink/Huber jointly chosen with Schwarzkopf/Fischer. Caveats: the panel was tiny (critics Martine Dumont-Mergeay of La Libre Belgique and musicologist Jean-Marc Onkelinx, host Paul-Antoine Patin), and a commenter on the very post preferred Ludwig 'au bord des larmes' over Fink ('confondante detresse interieure'). (2) klassik-prisma.de's 28-version comparison: 4/5 stars — 'die Stimme erinnert an die von Seefried, weniger emotionale Anteilnahme' (voice recalls Seefried's, less emotional involvement) — explicitly BELOW its five 5-star versions: Schwarzkopf/Fischer 1952, Schwarzkopf/Parsons 1973, Ludwig/Parsons ~1961, Janowitz/Gage 1977, Zomer/Schoonderwoerd. (3) Classics Today: 'Highly recommended', Fink 'deserves a place among the top-tier interpreters of German song', and on Gretchen specifically she 'builds the climax with a tone color that speaks volumes of regret and longing'. (4) OpusKlassiek (Aart van der Wal, Nov 2008): negative — in Gretchen Fink 'lijkt minder bij de tekst betrokken' (seems less engaged with the text), vibrato mars purity, prefers Ameling; also flags over-loud mastering. (5) A further mixed notice (surfaced in search snippets) calls it 'decidedly chaste, classically restrained Schubert' that 'underinflects and skates over many expressive opportunities'. (6) Gramophone reviewed the disc (May 2008, gramophone.co.uk/reviews/schubert-lieder) but the text sits behind Cloudflare and could not be retrieved. Separating PR from substance: the BBC Music Mag/Sunday Telegraph superlatives are classic label-circulated quotes; the blind-test co-win is real independent acclaim; but note the pattern that two independent continental critics (klassik-prisma, OpusKlassiek) independently fault emotional distance in this exact song.

The Topic upload sDacxcZdPYU is the durable replacement, but I did not test whether Topic uploads embed in the site's player in all regions (label-fed content sometimes carries embed/region restrictions). 2) Also note: a music.youtube search result (Nz8NugKVFS4) that looks like the Fink track is actually on the ELISABETH SCHWARZKOPF Topic channel — an easy mis-attribution trap I caught via oEmbed. 3) The blind-test credential is real but thin: two critics plus a host, and a joint (not sole) win. 4) Two independent critics (klassik-prisma: 'weniger emotionale Anteilnahme'; OpusKlassiek: 'seems less engaged with the text') separately fault exactly the quality — obsessive emotional escalation — that this song lives on. 5) The Gramophone review text could not be retrieved (Cloudflare), and the Sunday Telegraph/BBC Music Mag superlatives reached me only via a fan upload's description, i.e. through the label-PR quote pipeline. 6) HM Gold physical reissue unverified. 7) Recording date 'September 2007' rests on retailer metadata (Presto/audaud), not the booklet itself — low risk but not primary-source confirmed.
verdict: Strength 6/10. Honest comparison: this recording's standing does NOT rest on marketing alone — a blind panel that could not see the famous names still picked it alongside Schwarzkopf/Fischer out of eight versions spanning 1947-2017, which is exactly the kind of evidence the project's PR-skepticism rule asks for, and Classics Today's independent praise of the Gretchen climax corroborates it. Vocal condition at the recording is not a concern despite her age (52): the voice was fresh, even Seefried-like. BUT under the project's old-masters-first rules it cannot claim a top-4 slot: klassik-prisma's 28-version survey rates it 4/5, explicitly below Schwarzkopf/Fischer 1952, Schwarzkopf/Parsons 1973, Ludwig/Parsons ~1961 and Janowitz/Gage 1977 — the very old masters the project prioritizes — and two independent critics fault reduced textual/emotional engagement in this specific song, where mounting obsession is the whole drama. Verdict: the strongest verified MODERN candidate for D 118 — better documented and better available (official harmonia mundi Topic upload) than Fleming, Bonney, Isokoski or Dessay — and a defensible choice for a deliberate 'one modern version in modern sound' fifth slot; not competitive for slots 1-4 against Schwarzkopf, Ludwig and Janowitz. Include only if the editorial concept wants a modern-recording representative; if the top-5 is purely merit-by-project-rules, the old masters crowd it out.
